content: In health facilities, lengthy and intensive pre-test counseling and individual risk assessments are not recommended as they can create barriers to service delivery, consume significant healthcare worker time and resources, and provide minimal benefit to clients. Instead, pre-test information can be delivered through individual or group sessions, as well as media such as posters, brochures, websites, and short videos in waiting areas. Efforts to increase demand and utilization of HTS are outlined in the 2015 WHO Consolidated Guidelines for HIV Testing Services. Pre-test information for individuals receiving HIV testing should include clear details about the benefits of testing, the implications of positive and negative results, available services for those diagnosed as HIV-positive (including access to antiretroviral therapy or ART), prevention options, partner testing, confidentiality of results, the right to refuse testing, potential risks (especially for those with stigmatized behaviors), and the opportunity to ask questions. Informed consent for testing is essential. Post-test counseling for individuals who test HIV-negative should include an explanation of the result, methods to prevent HIV acquisition, provision of condoms and lubricants with guidance on their use, the importance of knowing the HIV status of sexual partners, and information about partner and couples testing services. Those with recent risky behavior should be advised to return for repeat testing in four weeks, and ongoing risk should prompt testing every 6–12 months. Pregnant women testing negative in high-prevalence settings should be encouraged to have their partners tested, as incident HIV during pregnancy or postpartum increases the risk of mother-to-child transmission. For individuals testing HIV-positive, post-test counseling should include an explanation of the result, time to process the diagnosis, and support for coping with emotions. Immediate concerns should be addressed, and clients should be helped to identify supportive individuals in their social network. Risks of intimate partner violence and mental health issues, such as depression or suicide, should be assessed, with referrals to appropriate services. Information on ART, its health benefits, and its role in reducing HIV transmission should be provided, along with details on accessing ART. A specific date for follow-up and active referral to HIV care should be arranged if same-day enrollment is not possible. Prevention of HIV transmission, including the use of condoms and lubricants, should be discussed. Testing for sexual partners, children, and family members should be encouraged, and referrals to prevention, counseling, and support services should be made as needed. For pregnant women testing HIV-positive, counseling should include discussions about childbirth plans, the importance of delivering in a health facility, the use of antiretroviral drugs for maternal and infant health, partner testing, and screening for tuberculosis and other infections. Maternal nutrition, infant feeding options, and HIV testing for the infant should also be addressed. Inconclusive test results, which occur when initial reactive results are not confirmed or when conflicting results arise, should prompt retesting after 14 days. These results can be confusing and stressful for clients and challenging for providers to explain. Most inconclusive results are resolved with retesting. Post-test counseling for key populations, such as people who inject drugs, may require intensified follow-up and linkage to harm reduction services, including opioid substitution therapy and needle and syringe programs. Adolescents testing HIV-positive should receive tailored advice, linkage to care, mental health services, and sexual and reproductive health services. To improve the quality and efficiency of HTS, WHO recommends integrating HTS with other health services, decentralizing HTS to primary care and community settings, and task-sharing responsibilities with trained lay providers. Integration with services such as tuberculosis, maternal and child health, and harm reduction programs can increase convenience and uptake of testing. Decentralization can reduce transportation costs and waiting times, though it may not always be appropriate or efficient in certain settings. Task-sharing addresses healthcare worker shortages by redistributing tasks to trained lay providers, who can safely and effectively conduct HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests. Community-based HIV testing services are essential for reaching first-time testers and those who rarely use clinical services, including key populations. These services can be offered in community sites, schools, workplaces, and places of worship, or through mobile units. HIV self-testing (HIVST) allows individuals to collect a specimen, perform a test, and interpret the result privately. While it does not provide a definitive diagnosis, reactive results require confirmatory testing. Self-testing can extend HTS to those unable or unwilling to attend traditional services. Providers distributing self-test kits should advise individuals with non-reactive results to retest if they have ongoing risk. Self-testing may yield false-negative results in individuals on ART, particularly with oral fluid-based tests. Facilityor community-based HTS is recommended for those uncertain about conducting self-tests. Early infant diagnosis (EID) is critical for identifying HIV in infants, as untreated HIV-infected infants face high mortality in the first year of life. Virological testing using nucleic acid testing (NAT) is required for infants under 18 months due to the persistence of maternal HIV antibodies. All HIV-exposed infants should undergo virological testing at 4–6 weeks of age, with ART initiated immediately for those with positive results. Testing should align with immunization schedules to maximize uptake. Infants with reactive serological assays at nine months should undergo virological testing to confirm infection and determine ART needs. In summary, comprehensive HTS approaches, including preand post-test counseling, integration with other health services, decentralization, task-sharing, community-based services, and self-testing, are essential for improving HIV diagnosis, prevention, and care. Early testing and treatment initiation, particularly for infants and key populations, are critical for reducing HIV-related morbidity and mortality.
